title: Ebola Outbreak: Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda - Externl Update 4 June 2026
content:
Overview of the outbreak

• A new Ebola virus disease outbreak was declared in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) on 15 May and as of 2 June, WHO has reported 344 confirmed cases, six recoveries and 60 deaths, including two internally displaced people (IDPs) in eastern DRC. The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccines or therapeutics.

• Since 17 May when WHO declared the outbreak a Public Health Emergency of International Concern, the virus has spread from Bunia in Ituri province to North Kivu and South Kivu, affecting 24 health zones, many of them located close to refugee camps and sites across the three provinces.

• More than 2 million forcibly displaced people including 230,000 refugees and asylum-seekers live in the areas at highest risk in eastern DRC. Persistent conflict and insecurity in the area has severely impacted local infrastructure and health systems, reduced humanitarian access, and disrupted protection services. This has increased protection risks for forcibly displaced people, weakened their inclusion in health surveillance systems and reduced access to healthcare.

• Uganda has also reported 15 confirmed Ebola cases, including two recoveries and one death. While no forcibly displaced people are among the reported cases, exposure risks remain significant.

• In Uganda, some reception and transit centres are operating above capacity. UNHCR and its partners are working to decongest these facilities through relocations to settlements.

title: Iran-Afghanistan - Returns Emergency Response #30 (as of 6 June 2026)
content:
Context

On 20 March 2025, headcount slips for an estimated 2 million Afghans in Iran expired, after which the Government introduced a regularization and return scheme, requiring slip holders to undergo assessments to determine whether they can remain.

Since then, returns have increased significantly. In 2025, more than 1.9 million Afghans returned or were deported from Iran – many not by choice. In 2026, a further 311,200 Afghans have returned. These large-scale returns are placing pressure on basic services, housing and livelihoods in Afghanistan, straining host communities and increasing the risks of instability and onward movement.

At the same time, hostilities across Asia and the Middle East since 28 February 2026 have further compounded the situation. As one of the largest refugee-hosting countries in the region, Iran is facing growing pressure amid rising humanitarian needs, highlighting the need for flexible and sustained support.

title: Central African Republic: Situation Report No. 71, as of 9 June, 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • Insecurity leads to an increase in basic commodity prices in Zemio
  • 850 returnees receive multisectoral assistance in Ouham-Pendé
  • Bria: Humanitarian actors assess urgent needs of CAR returnees from Sudan

GENERAL CONTEXT

Haut-Mbomou Prefecture – South-East

  • For over a year, the deterioration of the security situation in Haut-Mbomou has had a severe humanitarian impact on civilian populations, particularly in Zemio and surrounding areas. Movement restrictions and insecurity along key routes have reduced physical access to markets and disrupted supply chains. As a result, prices of staple foods and essential goods have sharply increased—up to threefold for some items—significantly reducing household purchasing power and access to adequate food. The scarcity of goods in local markets, combined with high prices, limits household access to food, especially among the most vulnerable, and worsens the risk of food insecurity, while encouraging negative coping strategies. In Haut-Mbomou, 32,000 people don’t always know whether they will have enough food, due to the prevailing security situation and other factors.

HUMANITARIAN NEEDS AND RESPONSE

Multi-sector

Haute-Kotto Prefecture – Central

  • On 3 June, a joint needs assessment mission composed of the Comité international d’aide d’urgence et de développement (CIAUD), Plan International, United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) and OCHA visited Ngoubi village, 18 km from Bria, to assess the needs of spontaneous returnees from Sudan. This mission follows the arrival in Bria on 22 May of CAR returnees from Sudan, after a journey of approximately 20 days under difficult conditions, during which one person died. A total of 31 households (130 people) were registered. Priority needs identified include food assistance, livelihood support (including cassava cuttings), shelter and essential household items, access to health services, education for children, Water, hygiene and sanitation (WASH) and protection. Efforts are ongoing to mobilize assistance to address these needs rapidly.

Food Security

Mbomou Prefecture – South-East

  • From 1 to 5 June, the NGO Action communautaire pour la reconstruction et le développement durable (ACRED), with support from the Humanitarian Fund, distributed agricultural inputs to 150 vulnerable households, including host communities and IDPs, in Pombolo. Distributed inputs included seeds (groundnuts, paddy rice, maize, squash), tools and other items (hoes, machetes, tarpaulins, basins, and empty sacks). This distribution is part of an emergency project aimed at supporting early recovery for households facing food insecurity.

title: ACAPS Thematic Report: Ukraine - January–April 2026 humanitarian access update, 11 June 2026
content:
OVERVIEW

Between January–April 2026, humanitarian access in frontline oblasts remained challenging following shifts in the frontline. After frontline movement led to increased shelling, particularly in the east, raions in these areas have seen humanitarian access deteriorate. Access breakdown and service disruptions continue to develop in areas further beyond the frontline, with technological advancements expanding drone reach and placing an even wider region under threat of strikes.

This reporting period saw significant challenges in access to energy, heating, and other civilian services, as freezing weather conditions – the coldest in 15 years at −20°C – increased needs for electricity and heating sources. Persistent Russian strikes on energy infrastructure outpaced repairs, widening the gap between civilians’ service needs and the accessibility of those services and hampering humanitarian response capacity.

In Donetska oblast, Druzhkivka, Kramatorsk, and Sloviansk in Kramatorskyi raion became increasingly central to both military defence efforts and humanitarian action as the frontline moved as close as 15km away. These cities, which contain the largest remaining population centres in Ukrainian-controlled Donetska oblast, have experienced some of the most significant increases in aerial attacks and shifting frontlines from January–April 2026, increasing civilian evacuations and affecting humanitarians’ ability to consistently access these populations.

Kherson city and riverbank areas in Khersonskyi and Beryslavskyi raions continue to experience persistent strikes. Since January, the range of these strikes has slowly been increasing, with more attacks reaching as far as 25km and a very limited number reaching as far as 40km beyond the river. These attacks are raising the already high level of humanitarian action access severity within these regions. New Russian tactics, including the increased use of petal mines in Kherson city, are increasing the daily threat level throughout the city in both road and pedestrian areas, affecting civilian and humanitarian movements through the city.

Russian attacks on transport and logistics hubs persisted at elevated rates through the reporting period, reducing operational continuity for civilians, humanitarians, and military alike, particularly in the east and north. Because of this targeting, general insecurity in these areas also increased, hindering safe humanitarian access. Attacks have affected major roadways and transit points in places such as Barvinkove, Lozova, Pavlohrad, Romny, and Sloviansk, making movement more difficult and necessitating the use of alternative roads and routes for safer humanitarian passage.

title: DRC Situational Report #6 Jonglei Emergency (8 June 2026)
content:
The situation across Jonglei remains fragile and volatile, with localized violence and increasing humanitarian needs. Intercommunal tensions and recurrent cattle raiding, often a key driver of localized violence and retaliation cycles, further compound insecurity, contributing to a highly volatile environment, particularly in areas between frontlines.

Humanitarian needs remain acute across Jonglei.
Continued displacement and returns – particularly in Akobo – are placing pressure on already limited services.
Food insecurity remains high, with increased admissions to nutrition programmes. Protection risks are widespread, including GBV, family separation, abductions, and psychosocial distress. Access to basic services such as health,WASH, and protection remains limited, especially in hard-to-reach areas.

Recent assessments across Chuil, Yuai, and Paguir highlight early and forced marriage, gaps in MHPSS and child protection, limited inclusive governance structures, and urgent needs for dignity kits and targeted support to women and girls.

title: DRC: Ebola BVD Outbreak: LTC Situation Report (Telecoms) #2 (Reporting period: 04 – 10 June 2026)
content:
This situation report provides updates on the Ebola Bundibugyo Virus Disease (BVD) Outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). It outlines the planned telecommunications activities of the Logistics & Telecommunications Cluster1 (LTC) to support the ongoing humanitarian response.

Summary Points

• Telecommunications in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) remain constrained by limited infrastructure, uneven coverage, unreliable power supply, and high operating costs. In Ituri and other Ebola-affected areas, these challenges create critical connectivity gaps that hinder coordination, surveillance, and timely response.

• Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) has received 150 satellite terminals in Bunia, with LTC Telecoms supporting distribution and installation to strengthen connectivity at priority response sites. Coordinated deployment is essential to ensure equipment is used where needs are greatest.

• The International Telecommunication Union (ITU) has activated a Disaster Connectivity Map (DCM) campaign for Ituri and surrounding areas, also available on LogIE. The platform provides regularly updated mobile network data, helping identify stable coverage and connectivity gaps to support operations.

title: Philippines: 7.8M Sarangani Earthquake Flash Update No. 2 (As of 10 June 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • A magnitude 7.8 earthquake struck 32 km offshore west of Maasim, Sarangani on 08 June at 7:37 a.m. local time. The Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHIVOLCS) has since recorded more than 2,000 aftershocks, with further seismic activity expected.
  • Government figures indicate 45 people have died, 487 have been injured, and 17 remain missing. The number of affected people has risen to approximately 197,750 (43,716 families) across Regions IX, XI, XII, and BARMM.
  • At least 25,000 people remain displaced, including around 16,000 sheltering in 31 evacuation centres, while many others are staying in makeshift shelters outside damaged homes due to continued aftershocks.
  • Widespread damage has been reported, with 7,866 houses affected (1,596 destroyed and 6,720 partially damaged) and infrastructure losses estimated at US $9.2 million. Damage to roads and other infrastructure is constraining access to affected and isolated communities.
  • Essential services remain disrupted. General Santos International Airport is closed to commercial flights, power outages persist in several areas, and access to some municipalities and island communities remains limited due to damaged roads.
  • The Government continues to lead response efforts, with over 2,700 search and rescue personnel deployed and additional teams on standby. The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) has provided more than US $3.5 million worth of humanitarian assistance, while sectoral agencies are working to restore critical lifeline services.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

Two days after the magnitude 7.8 earthquake struck 32 km offshore west of Maasim, Sarangani Province, along the Cotabato Trench, the humanitarian impact continues to unfold across Mindanao. The earthquake, which had a depth of 33 km, has been followed by more than 2,000 aftershocks ranging from magnitude 1.2 to 6.4, according to the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHIVOLCS), with further aftershocks expected.

According to the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD), 197,750 people (43,716 families) have been affected across Regions IX, XI and XII, and the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM). Updated figures from the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (NDRRMC) indicate that 45 people have died and 487 have been injured, while 17 people remain missing. More than 25,000 people are currently displaced, including some 16,000 people sheltering in 31 evacuation centres. Although the number of people staying in evacuation centres has declined, field reports indicate that many affected families are continuing to stay in makeshift shelters outside their homes due to fear of ongoing aftershocks. Government authorities, civil society organizations and the private sector have mobilized to support affected cities and municipalities. Response efforts are ongoing to reach communities cut off by damaged road infrastructure.

title: WFP India Country Brief, June 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• On 23 May 2026, in Jharsuguda, Odisha, state ministers inaugurated the second standalone Grain ATM and announced a statewide scale-up, with expansion in other states—strengthening last-mile food access, transparency, and efficient public distribution nationwide.

title: UNHCR Middle East Situation: Emergency Update #20 as of 9 June 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

REGIONAL CONTEXT

Since late February, escalating hostilities in Iran and Lebanon have triggered humanitarian consequences with impact across the region, including refugee returns in adverse circumstances to Afghanistan and Syria. Events are unfolding against an already fragile humanitarian baseline, with over 31 million forcibly displaced people and recent returnees across the wider region prior to the current escalation (including Palestine refugees under UNRWA's mandate), alongside host communities under significant economic and social strain.

Inter agency emergency response is underway to address urgent needs. In Iran, the Flash Refugee Response Plan targets refugees and others in need of international protection alongside affected host communities. In Lebanon, a Flash Appeal complements the broader response under the Lebanon Response Plan to deliver life saving assistance and protection, including to Syrian refugees. In Afghanistan, the funding requirement for the returns response is outlined under the Humanitarian Needs & Response Plan.

UNHCR and partners have been working across countries neighbouring Iran to strengthen preparedness for possible large-scale refugee flows, in support of national authorities. Preparedness measures are in place, including border monitoring, reception and protection readiness, but these arrangements remain highly dependent on flexible and predictable funding in an increasingly constrained resource environment.

title: WFP Afghanistan Country Brief, June 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

Afghanistan is experiencing its highest levels of acute malnutrition on record: in 2026, acute malnutrition will impact 3.7 million children under five, including nearly a million impacted by severe acute malnutrition, as well as 1.2 million pregnant or breastfeeding women, according to IPC estimations. Many WFP-supported health clinics are facing a shortage of specialized nutritious foods and therefore unable to deliver life-saving treatment to malnourished children and women, leaving only a fraction of those in need able to access support.

Regional conflicts are exacerbating the humanitarian crisis in Afghanistan, with staple food prices rising by up to 30 percent and transport costs tripling amid rerouted supply chains to bypass Iran, increased fuel prices and continued border closures with Pakistan. These pressures are particularly acute for imported nutrition commodities, with the result that one million children will be denied food assistance this year.

Severe funding constraints have now forced WFP to halt cash assistance for returnees from Iran and Pakistan at all border crossing points, cutting off vital support to families arriving in highly vulnerable conditions and leaving response capacity insufficient to mount an immediate response, should another large-scale influx occur.

title: WFP Madagascar Country Brief May 2026
content:
• In April, WFP maintained malnutrition prevention activities across communes targeted under the 2025–2026 Lean Season response, despite suspension of unconditional assistance due to pipeline breaks. Nutritious food assistance reached 38,593 children under two and 32,159 pregnant and breastfeeding women, ensuring continuity of support to vulnerable groups.
  • Following Cyclones Fytia and Gezani, WFP provided emergency cash assistance to 142,162 people across the east and west, with two additional rounds planned.
  • To sustain lean season distributions and scale up cyclone recovery, WFP requires USD 24.4 million (May–October 2026), as current resources remain insufficient.

title: Kenya | Complex Emergency - 6 Month Operational Update - MDRKE068
content:
A. SITUATION ANALYSIS

Despite recent rainfall, the drought and food‑security crisis in Kenya remains severe and life‑threatening. Over three million people are still facing Crisis or Emergency levels of hunger, malnutrition rates remain critically high among children and pregnant and lactating women, and fragile livelihoods have not recovered. Seasonal gains in water and pasture are uneven and short‑lived, while depleted herds, high food prices, and reduced assistance continue to push vulnerable households toward irreversible losses.

Yet this Emergency Appeal is only 9 per cent funded at a time when needs are rising, not receding. Without urgent additional funding, KRCS and partners will be forced to limit coverage, shorten assistance cycles, and leave high‑risk communities without lifesaving food, water, nutrition, and health support. Timely donor investment now can prevent further deterioration, protect livelihoods, and save lives reducing the far higher costs of emergency escalation later in the year if action is delayed.

title: UNICEF Syria Humanitarian Situation Report (Euphrates Flooding), 08 June 2026
content:
Key figures As of 7 June 2026

17,000 people directly affected by the floods.

700 families displaced, representing around 2,000 children.

Thousands of children exposed to heightened risks.

49 water treatment plants out of service in Deir-ez-Zor and Raqqa Governorates.

Situation Update

While the water level of the Euphrates River has receded significantly across Aleppo, Deir-ez-Zor, and Raqqa governorates, and the flood wave is gradually stabilizing, the river flow remains at twice the seasonal average, putting children and their families at continuous risk and disrupting access to essential services and humanitarian assistance.

The flooding has already caused humanitarian impacts across communities located along the Euphrates. Approximately 3,400 households were affected, with over 700 families displaced. Reports also indicate the death of nine people by drowning, including children, due to the sudden rise in water, and the flooding of multiple informal settlements. Around 20,000 dunums of agricultural land have been flooded, and poultry farms and fishponds have been damaged.

Critical infrastructure has sustained extensive damage. Several bridges and river crossings have collapsed or are inaccessible, severely disrupting humanitarian and commercial access between the two banks of the river. Water infrastructure has also been severely damaged, with multiple water stations flooded, but the repair efforts have been tremendous. As for Raqqa Governorate, out of 86 affected water stations, only 3 remain out of service, but 46 water treatment plants remain out of service in Deir-ez-Zor Governorate. The Water Establishment and UNICEF’s support enabled the continuation of operations at the Euphrates Water Treatment Plant, which supplies water to approximately 400,000 people, despite the collapse of protective embankments and flooding on the plant premises.

Children continue to face heightened vulnerabilities as families recover from displacement, damaged shelters, and disruptions to basic services. Protection risks remain a key concern, including the risk of drowning in residual floodwaters and increased exposure to Unexploded Ordnance (UXO), as floodwaters may have shifted explosive remnants into residential and agricultural areas. Additional protection concerns include increased risks of violence against children, psychosocial distress, and challenges faced by families who have lost civil documentation required to access essential services and assistance. Damage to infrastructure and public facilities may also continue to affect children's access to education.

The flooding has occurred against a backdrop of ongoing public health challenges, including continued measles transmission in several areas. While floodwaters are receding, deteriorated WASH conditions continue to increase the risk of waterborne disease outbreaks and may further exacerbate disease transmission among already vulnerable populations. Disease surveillance in affected locations has reported cases of acute watery diarrhea and confirmed measles cases in the last few months, underscoring the need for sustained public health interventions.

Despite the gradual decline in water levels, continued humanitarian support remains essential to address immediate needs and prevent secondary impacts on affected populations. Timely assistance – including access to safe water, health and immunization services, child protection support, mine and child protection risk awareness, and cash assistance – will be critical to helping families recover and reducing the risks faced by children and caregivers. Without sustained support, affected communities may face prolonged disruptions to essential services and increased vulnerability after years of protracted crisis.

UNICEF and partners continue to coordinate closely with local authorities and humanitarian actors to monitor the evolving situation, assess remaining needs, and support response and early recovery efforts across affected governorates.

title: Somalia Weekly Weather Forecast - Valid From 9 to 15 June 2026
content:
Forecast Highlight:

• Somalia has entered the Hagaa dry inter-season with the country likely to remain dry during the week from 9 to 15 June except for light rainfall forecast along the southern coastal margin (Lower Juba, Middle Juba, Lower Shabelle, Banadir); and Togdheer and Sanaag highland areas

• The current Shabelle upstream flow presents no flood risk at current levels but should be monitored as it propagates to Bulo Burte and Jowhar during the forecast period

• The May 2026 CDI confirms widespread Gu recovery across most of Somalia, but moderate-to-severe drought persists in central parts of Bay and coastal parts of both Bari and Sanaag

• High temperatures of above 35 °C are forecast across most parts; communities entering the Hagaa with residual drought face compounded heat, water stress, and livestock disease pressure

Review Summary:

• During 2–8 June 2026, rainfall was concentrated in northern Somaliland with isolated coastal showers in Lower Shabelle, confirming the weakening and cessation of Gu 2026 convective activity over most of Somalia

• Gu 2026 delivered above-normal cumulative rainfall over Somaliland and Jubaland, normal performance in central regions and below-normal performance in most parts of Puntland.

• A notable upstream pulse on the Shabelle River has been detected: Deefow rose by +1.56 m and Belet Weyne by +1.08 m to 4.58 m — well below the 6.50 m moderate flood level but the pulse is propagating downstream toward Bulo Burte and Jowhar

• Livelihood recovery lags behind meteorological improvement in many areas due to livestock disease, crop pests, conflict-related displacement, and residual drought in Bay and northeastern Bari

title: WFP Kyrgyz Republic Country Brief, June 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

The Kyrgyz Republic, a landlocked mountainous country, has seen steady economic growth but still faces development challenges and lower income levels than many other Asia nations. Rural communities make up around 60 percent of the 7.4 million population, with poverty affecting 26 percent nationwide (National Statistics Committee). Moreover, 43 percent cannot afford a nutritious diet (WFP Price Bulletin #98), while 75 percent rely on negative coping strategies such as debt or reduced spending on healthcare (WFP Food Security Update 2025). Malnutrition persists, with 21 percent of children under five with anemia (NIMAS).

Food security remains fragile due to heavy reliance on remittances, large-scale migrant returns, limited agricultural self‑sufficiency, high inflation, climate shocks, and recent regional geopolitical tensions affecting global energy, fertilizer and food markets.
With 93 percent of its territory covered by high mountains, the country is highly disaster‑prone, particularly to mudflows.

WFP supports government implementation of the National Development Programme 2030, the Mountain Agenda, Nationally Determined Contributions 3.0, and sectoral strategies, focusing on inclusive social protection, green economic growth, human capital development, disaster risk reduction and climate resilience. In collaboration with partners, WFP aims to transform food systems and livelihoods, ensuring that economic growth leads to greater resilience and equitable opportunities, particularly in the country's most remote and mountain areas.

title: Ukraine: Humanitarian Response Update, 8 June 2026
content: Through its Emergency and Early Recovery Response Plan for 2026–2028, the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) is targeting 239 844 rural families and small-scale farmers affected by the ongoing war. With a total funding requirement of USD 193 million, the plan combines urgent agricultural support with early recovery measures to help sustain food production and rural livelihoods. During the first half of 2026, FAO has supported over 11 000 rural families with seed potatoes, vegetable seeds, young poultry, cash and voucher assistance, including support for animal feed and fuelwood. In parallel, more than 600 farmers received agricultural input vouchers for sowing campaigns and mine action-related recovery, modular storage units, and grant support for farm development. This assistance helped them maintain production, safely store harvested grain, invest in value chains and resume agricultural activities in affected areas.

title: WFP Dominican Republic Country Brief, June 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

• The Dominican Republic, like other Small Island Developing States in the Caribbean, is highly exposed to severe weather events such as hurricanes, flooding, and droughts, which disrupt livelihoods, damage infrastructure, and strain food systems. Ecosystem degradation further reduces natural protection against extreme events. Around 25% of households are highly vulnerable to climate shocks, disproportionately affecting poor and hazard‑prone communities.
Territorial inequalities leave rural and border provinces with fewer opportunities and higher poverty rates, while 53.4% of employment is informal. Global food price volatility, dependence on remittances, and localized migration pressures compound these risks, intersecting with persistent micronutrient deficiencies and the double burden of malnutrition disproportionately affecting women, children, and excluded groups. These vulnerabilities are exacerbated by global market instability linked to the Middle East crisis, driving food price volatility, energy cost increases, and supply chain disruption, raising concern for national food security and household resilience.

• WFP’s strategy links national planning with local action to address recurrent shocks systemically. Evidence and data guide interventions, building government capacity so central decisions translate into community protection. Climate services and risk management tools are embedded in social protection through local networks, enabling anticipatory action. Pre‑positioning, disaster risk finance, and logistics corridors ensure rapid response when systems are strained. Platforms such as ANACAONA and the DR–Haiti corridor exemplify collective resilience.

title: WFP Nepal Republic Country Brief, June 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Following the March 2026 elections, a new reform-oriented government has accelerated institutional changes, creating opportunities for stronger systems and ownership while requiring adaptive partner engagement.

• GDP growth rose from 1.9 percent in 2023 to 3.9 percent in 2024, driven by remittances, hydropower, agriculture and tourism, but is projected to slow to 2.3 percent in fiscal year 2026 (FY26) amid Middle East impacts.

• In October 2024, 16.5 percent of the population was food insecure - 0.9 percent higher than March 2024 but 6.4 percent lower than the April 2020 peak - while 4.81 million people had inadequate food consumption, with stable food prices overall but higher costs in mountain regions, which worsened access challenges.

• The 2026 monsoon in Nepal has shown a delayed and below-average onset so far, raising concerns for agriculture and food security, with WFP closely monitoring the situation and ready to support as needed.

title: WFP Lao People's Democratic Republic Country Brief, June 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• The Minister of Health approved a Ministerial Agreement on national rice fortification standards, effective July 2026, marking important progress toward government-led scale-up of rice fortification to improve nutrition outcomes nationwide.

• WFP food security monitoring for the first quarter of 2026 indicates increasing pressure on vulnerable households: o Food insecurity rose to 9 percent in Q1 2026, up from 8 percent in late 2025, as vulnerable households depleted harvest stocks ahead of the monsoon. o Price increases linked to the Middle East crisis, compounded by 2025 weather shocks, sharply worsened food security since Q4 2025 in Sekong (22 to 31 percent) and Oudomxay (9 to 17 percent).

IN NUMBERS

168,100 people assisted in May 2026

49% Male

51% Female

125 mt food distributed, benefiting 163,000 students and supporters in schools

USD 3.31 m required in the next six months (June – November 2026)

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• The Lao People's Democratic Republic is a landlocked, least developed nation with a population of 7.8 million. As of 2024/2025, about 15 percent of its people live below the national poverty line of USD 1.10 per day. Poverty dropped by over half in the past two decades. The 2024 Global Hunger Index rates the country's hunger as “moderate.”

• Climate change is a major challenge for rural population and the country is vulnerable due to its low adaptability and heavy dependence on climatesensitive natural resources. Changing climate patterns, limited access to markets and varied livelihoods further worsen the situation in remote upland areas, where over 20 percent of households are food insecure (national average: 10 percent).
Chronic malnutrition affects 33 percent of children under five, while micronutrient deficiencies are high and overnutrition is on the rise in urban areas.

• WFP has been present in Lao PDR since 1976.

title: Public Health Situation Analysis (PHSA) - Yemen ( 22 May 2026)
content:
Yemen enters 2026 at a critical tipping point, with 22.3 million people in need of humanitarian assistance and protection. Surging needs, significant funding cuts, and shrinking access are forcing partners to scale back life-saving support. Without urgent action, lives will be lost, communities will destabilize, and essential systems will edge closer to collapse. A well-funded response and unimpeded humanitarian access are critical to prevent Yemen from sliding into a deeper catastrophe.[i]

Nearly 5 million people are experiencing IPC Phase 3 or above (Crisis or worse) conditions between March and May 2026, with 1.4 million people experiencing IPC Phase 4 (Emergency).[ii] Yemen faces widespread outbreaks of vaccine -preventable diseases, including circulating vaccine -derived poliovirus type 2 (cVDPV2), acute watery diarrhea (AWD)/cholera, measles, diphtheria, dengue fever and malaria, exacerbated by low vaccination rates, misinformation.[iii]

Against a backdrop of increasing needs, the humanitarian response in 2025 operated under severe and unprecedented funding shortages, with the Yemen 2025 HNRP funded at only 29%, forcing clusters to scale down or suspend critical life‑saving services across sectors. As of May 2026, reduced funding has resulted in a reduction of nutrition services by up to 63%.[iv] Over 450 health facilities, including 76 hospitals, have closed in the last year.[v]

WHO is appealing for US$ 38.8 million to deliver life-saving emergency health assistance to 10.5 million people across Yemen in 2026, as the country enters another year of protracted conflict, disease outbreaks, climate shocks and deepening humanitarian needs.[vi]

The humanitarian context in Yemen in 2025 was defined by a spiral of regional escalation and cross-border conflict; a collapse of the operational space in areas under the control of the de facto authorities (DfA) in Sana’a; and a fragmenting political landscape in areas under the internationally recognized Government (IRG) of Yemen. [vii]

Since 2014, Yemen has been engulfed in violent conflict. Critical infrastructure – including water, sanitation, education, health, and transport – has been damaged or destroyed, severely constraining public services and resilience. Despite substantial humanitarian and development aid, the situation in Yemen has continued to deteriorate, becoming increasingly entrenched due to deeply rooted political dynamics.

By 2019, it had reversed human development by 21 years, and if the conflict continues until 2030, the developmental setback could extend to nearly four decades, more than one-and-a-half generations.[viii] Despite limited large-scale conflict between the parties of the ongoing civil conflict, Yemen was ranked the 5th least peaceful country in the world; the result of continued internal instability combined with growing entanglement in external conflict.[ix]

Escalating conflict in the Middle East has spillover risks for Yemen.[x] In March 2026, Ansar Allah began to engage in the regional war by launching military attacks against Israel.[xi] Renewed hostilities are already drawing forces into regional fighting. Strikes on Yemen may trigger displacement, civilian casualties, and damage to vital infrastructure, including ports and storage facilities, deepening humanitarian needs nationwide. [xii]

title: WFP Tajikistan Country Brief, June 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Tajikistan is a landlocked, mountainous country with a population of 10.27 million, growing at 2 percent yearly, the highest rate in Eastern Europe and Central Asia. Half of the population is under 25 years, and a quarter resides in cities (TAJSTAT, 2020).

• Nutrition outcomes have improved substantially since 2023: stunting among children under five declined from 26 percent in 2012 to 14 percent in 2023, while wasting dropped from 10 percent in 2012 to 6 percent by 2017 and remained at 6 percent in 2023 (TDHS, 2023).

• Tajikistan’s economy remains strong, with Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growing above 8 percent in 2024 and early 2025, supported by remittances, services, and industrial activity, while inflation remains low. However, the economy remains highly exposed to external shocks, as remittances account for nearly half of GDP and export performance continues to be weak.

• Poverty levels have declined from 21.7 percent in 2022 to 20.4 percent in 2023, with over onethird of households experiencing upward mobility, driven mainly by remittances and rising labor incomes in services and agriculture.
However, inequality and rural vulnerabilities persist due to limited job creation, low labor force participation—especially among women— and ongoing climate and economic risks.

title: Afghanistan: Weekly Market Report: Issue 298: Week 1 – June 2026
content:
Key Highlights

Exchange Rate and Trade Dynamics:

• During the first week of June, the Afghani exchange rate remained stable at AFN 63.8/USD, showing no change from the previous week. The Afghani continues to remain stronger than both last year (+9%) and the three-year average (+16%), helping to moderate imported inflationary pressures.

• Domestic markets continued to operate normally with generally adequate commodity availability, supported by ongoing domestic harvests, seasonal market arrivals, and sustained trade flows through regional corridors. However, transportation costs, regional trade uncertainties, and high dependence on imports continue to expose domestic supply chains to external market and geopolitical risks.

Food Items:

• Overall, national average food prices showed a generally stable trend during the first week of June, with slight week-on-week declines across major staple food items.

• Compared to last year, most food commodities continue to remain above their respective levels, particularly wheat grain (+12%), wheat flour (high-price +7%; low-price +10%), rice (high-quality +31%; low-quality +34%), cooking oil (+3%), sugar (+24%), and salt (+10%). Conversely, pulses (-12%) and bread (-4%) remained below last year's levels.

Vegetables:

• Vegetable prices continued to ease during the first week of June, largely driven by improved seasonal availability and increased domestic supply.

• Tomato prices recorded a significant weekly decline (-12.3%), continuing the downward trend observed in recent weeks. Onion and potato prices show negligible changes from last week, reflecting stable market conditions.

• Compared to last year, potato prices remain substantially above last year's levels (+44%), while tomato prices remain moderately higher (+6%). In contrast, onion prices continue to remain significantly below last year (-24%).

Non-Food Items:

• Diesel prices remained broadly stable during the week (+0.4%) and remains modestly above last year (+4%).

• Fertilizer prices (DAP and Urea) showed negligible week-on-week increases, while they remain significantly higher than last year, particularly DAP (+16%) and urea (+46%), continuing to exert pressure on agricultural production costs. Meanwhile, improved seed (-0.3%) and animal feed (-1.0%) recorded slight declines and remained relatively stable overall.

Livestock and Labour Market:

• The price of a one-year-old live female sheep declined by 6.8% during the week following elevated demand in the lead-up to Eid-ul-Adha. Despite the weekly decline, sheep prices remain broadly in line with last year and slightly above the three-year average.

• Labour market conditions remained weak. While the casual labour wage remained stable at AFN 304/day, labour availability declined to 1.9 days per week. Labour availability remains substantially below both last year (-20%) and the three-year average (-20%), highlighting continued challenges in income-earning opportunities for vulnerable households who are dependent on daily wage labour.

title: Argentina: Flood - DREF Final Report (MDRAR023)
content:
Description of the Event
Bahia Blanca District, Province of Buenos Aires.
Date of event
07-03-2025
What happened, where and when?

On 6 March 2025, the National Meteorological Service of Argentina issued an Orange Alert for storms for the southern region of the Province of Buenos Aires, warning of a dangerous event for society, life, property and the environment. Municipal authorities and community institutions took preventive measures, such as the temporary suspension of classes, the cancellation of outdoor activities and the reinforcement of risk communication.

During the early morning of 7/3/2025, the district of Bahía Blanca, on the southern coast of the province, experienced intense and continuous rains that accumulated between 300 and 350 mm of water, an event that exceeded the 100-year recurrence period. In view of the worsening forecast, the National Meteorological Service raised the alert to Red Level. This caused the Napostá stream, which crosses the city, to overflow, affecting approximately 70% of the area. Other local watercourses, such as the Maldonado stream, also overflowed, exacerbating the situation and leaving the city in a state of emergency.

The flooding caused significant damage to residential, commercial, and utility infrastructure, affecting homes, light poles, walls, trees, and signs. In addition, essential services were disrupted, including medical care, transportation, electricity, gas, fuel, telecommunications, and
water supply.

The urban and peri-urban areas of Bahía Blanca were the most affected, especially the towns of General Cerri and Ingeniero White, where pre-existing drainage conditions and high levels of vulnerability aggravated the situation. In General Cerri, material losses severely impacted families dependent on informal work, horticultural and rural production, generating a significant social impact.

In this context, the emergency gained international visibility and was reported in the international media. Following this situation, on 12 March 2025, the Senate declared the province of Buenos Aires, especially the municipalities of Bahía Blanca and Coronel Rosales, an emergency zone and a disaster situation for a period of 180 days due to the floods.

title: Guatemala | Drought: Early Action Protocol Activation (EAP No.: EAP2023GT03, Operation No.: MDRGT023), 9 June 2026
content:
EARLY ACTION PROTOCOL ACTIVATION

Activation Overview

The Guatemalan Red Cross has activated its Early Action Protocol for drought.

Based on the monitoring and technical analysis conducted by the National Institute of Seismology, Volcanology, Meteorology and Hydrology (INSIVUMEH), the activation of the Early Action Protocol (EAP) for drought is hereby reported, due to the fulfilment of the two triggers established in the approved protocol.

The activation is supported by the following technical criteria:

First trigger: INSIVUMEH forecasts the occurrence of an El Niño event in the Niño 3.4 region for the next three months, with a 70 per cent probability, according to the forecasts issued by the International Research Institute for Climate and Society (IRI) from June onwards.

Second trigger: INSIVUMEH has issued its seasonal precipitation forecast for the June-July-August period, indicating a 50 per cent probability that rainfall will be below the first tercile, or the 33rd percentile. This represents below-normal precipitation conditions and a significant increase in drought risk in the prioritized areas.

According to INSIVUMEH’s technical analysis, more than half of the national territory shows below-normal precipitation outlooks for the June-July-August quarter, particularly in the Dry Corridor and other areas vulnerable to water deficits. This situation, combined with the high probability of conditions associated with the El Niño phenomenon developing, increases the risk of impacts on food security, agricultural livelihoods and access to water for the most vulnerable populations.

In view of the above, the Early Action Protocol is officially activated, with the objective of implementing anticipatory actions aimed at reducing humanitarian impacts on the most vulnerable populations, particularly in relation to food security, livelihoods, access to water, health and protection.

Targeting of early action

The planned actions will be implemented in coordination with national authorities, humanitarian actors and prioritized communities, in accordance with the operational procedures and coordination mechanisms established in the EAP. The intervention will target the most vulnerable families that may be affected by the forecasted drought conditions, prioritizing those located in areas identified as having the highest exposure and vulnerability according to the protocol’s risk analysis.

The implementation of anticipatory actions will help strengthen community response capacity, reduce livelihood losses and contribute to mitigating the humanitarian impacts associated with the forecasted climate conditions.
Figure 1: Map of municipalities with meteorological drought risk indices for Guatemala.

The prioritized areas were identified by overlaying the EAP drought risk layer, which resulted from the integrated
analysis of hazard, exposure, vulnerability and response capacity, with the MJJ climate forecast map developed by
INSIVUMEH.

The selected municipalities correspond to those classified as having medium, high and very high-risk levels in the EAP
risk analysis, and which are also located within areas where rainfall is projected to be below the 33rd percentile for
the May-June-July period. The municipalities classified as very high risk are Chiquimula and Sacapulas, Quiché, while
the municipalities classified as high risk are Jalapa, Quetzaltenango and Retalhuleu.

title: Colombia | Droughts - Simplified Early Action Protocol Activation (EAP No.: sEAP2023CO01, Operation No.: MDRCO02)
content:
EARLY ACTION PROTOCOL ACTIVATION

Activation Overview

As part of the monthly monitoring process of the sEAP triggers—specifically, the three-month forecast of the percentage change in precipitation and the forecast of the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI), both provided by the Institute of Hydrology, Meteorology, and Environmental Studies (IDEAM) — it was found that for the month of April, the first trigger was met, but not the second; however, according to bulletins issued by IDEAM on May 20, there was evidence of the possibility that both triggers would be met. Therefore, IDEAM was asked to share the shapefiles containing the data associated with both triggers, which made it possible on Monday, June 1, to confirm that both triggers had been met through the cartographic analysis conducted (Figure 1).

According to an analysis based on data provided by IDEAM, three-month precipitation forecast indicates a more than 50% probability that precipitation will be below normal, and the SPI forecast, based on a moderate drought, shows values equal to or less than –1.4 for August 2026, in large areas of the departments of Tolima and Cesar. Early measures listed below are therefore expected to be implemented during the June–August 2026 quarter in Tolima and Cesar.

The early action will target:

  1. Individuals and families are susceptible to being affected by the shortage of water resources, limited access to water for human consumption.
  2. Individuals and families producing (agriculture and livestock) on a medium and small scale, who:
    • Are carrying out agricultural activity as their main source of income and subsistence and with a maximum of 5 productive hectares.
    • Havea livestock activity as their main source of income and subsistence and with a maximum of 5 heads of livestock.
  3. Individuals and families in areas susceptible to the proliferation of disease-transmitting vectors.

title: Syrian Arab Republic Euphrates River Floods 2026 - DREF Operation (MDRSY019)
content:
Description of the Event
Date of event
25-05-2026

What happened, where and when?

Since mid-May 2026, Syria has experienced severe flooding and rapidly rising water levels along the Euphrates River, primarily affecting Deir ez-Zor and Ar-Raqqa governorates in addition to Jarabulus from Aleppo governorate, following a sharp increase in water inflow from upstream areas in Türkiye. The increased inflow, reportedly reaching approximately 2,200 m³ per second, is mainly attributed to seasonal snowmelt and the opening of spillways at upstream dams.

As reservoir levels exceeded 97 per cent of storage capacity, authorities initiated emergency water management measures, including the opening of three spillway gates at the Euphrates Dam for the first time in more than three decades. Water discharge levels have significantly increased and may continue rising in the coming days if inflow persists.

The flooding has resulted in the displacement of at least 1,626 families in Deir ez-Zor Governorate, partial flooding of displacement sites in Ar-Raqqa, around 30 families, damage to agricultural land and disruption to critical infrastructure, including water stations and local access routes. Approximately 50 rural water stations in Deir ez-Zor and several additional stations in Ar-Raqqa are currently out of service or at risk due to inundation and restricted access.

Precautionary evacuations are ongoing in several high-risk communities located along the riverbanks, while local authorities and emergency actors continue to monitor water levels and implement protective measures to safeguard critical infrastructure and vulnerable populations.

The situation remains highly volatile, with authorities warning that additional spillway openings may become necessary should water inflow continue to increase, potentially leading to further flooding, displacement, service disruption, and humanitarian needs across affected areas along the Euphrates basin.

title: Syrian Arab Republic Emergency Mobility Tracking and Cross Border Monitoring Situation Update - Round 14 (08 June 2026)
content:
Population movements from Lebanon into the Syrian Arab Republic (hereafter referred to as Syria) continued to decline following the ceasefire announced on 17 April 2026, reflecting a significant reduction in displacement compared with the peak period of the conflict. Since the highest recorded level of arrivals on 27 April 2026 (153,087 individuals), approximately 32,738 Syrian and Lebanese nationals have returned to Lebanon, indicating a gradual stabilization of cross-border movements.

Between 2 March and 8 June, DTM recorded 120,349 arrivals across 1,234 locations across all 14 governorates of Syria. Syrian nationals accounted for the majority of those recorded, while Lebanese nationals represented less than one per cent of arrivals during the reporting period.

Cumulative monitoring data collected at the four Syrian–Lebanese border points of entry tracked by DTM recorded 418,589 movements into Syria as of 8 June. Syrian nationals constituted 97 per cent of all recorded movements, with Lebanese nationals accounting for the remaining 3 per cent. In addition, DTM reported the transit of 2,426 Lebanese nationals through Syrian territory towards Jordan.

Key informants (KIs) continued to report significant reintegration challenges among newly arrived households. The inability to secure stable work upon arrival has been compounded by high livings costs, undermining the purchasing power of returnees. Low-income families are particularly at risk of failing to meet their basic needs, compounded by reports of depleted savings as the situation continues. Although KIs reported that many returnees returned to homes they own, temporary housing pressure exists where those previously living in these homes had to vacate, or where families are hosted by relatives and friends. These pressures have strained local resources, fuelling social tensions and creating instability, reported particularly in the southern sub-districts and Al-Yarubiyah in Al-Hasakeh, where instances of kidnapping, theft, and housing/property disputes were common. KIs described the journey from Lebanon as difficult and costly, further compounding economic vulnerability upon arrival. KIs also cited cases of exploitation experienced along the route, causing persistent psychological stress among arrivals. The situation remains fluid, and DTM continues to monitor developments.

title: PHL: Earthquake - 06-2026 - 7.8 Magnitude Earthquake in Maasim, Sarangani #2 (2026-06-09)
content:
Description

At 7:37 AM on 8 June 2026, a magnitude 7.8 earthquake struck approximately 32 km south 04° west of Maasim, Sarangani, at a depth of 33 kilometers, affecting several areas in Mindanao. The Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHIVOLCS) recorded the strongest ground shaking at Intensity VII (Destructive) in General Santos City, with expected aftershocks and reported damages.

DOST-PHIVOLCS issued Tsunami Information No. 1 on 08 June 2026 at 7:37 AM, warning that coastal areas may experience tsunami wave heights of more than one meter above normal tide levels, which may be higher in enclosed bays and straits. Communities in Sarangani, Davao Occidental, Tawi-Tawi, Sulu, Basilan, Zamboanga del Sur, Zamboanga Sibugay, Sultan Kudarat, and South Cotabato were strongly advised to immediately evacuate to safer areas.

Based on reports from PRC Chapters, several structural damages were recorded. A total of two (2) structures totally collapsed in North Cotabato and General Santos City; four (4) structures sustained major damages in General Santos City, Davao City, and Sarangani; two (2) additional structures collapsed in General Santos City; four (4) structures sustained minor damages in Davao Oriental and Davao City; and one (1) incident of fallen debris was reported in Davao del Sur. Damaged structures included municipal halls, gyms, and commercial establishments.

A total of four (4) hospitals in Davao Oriental, South Cotabato, and General Santos City were also affected, sustaining minor to visible cracks and structural damages.

Additionally, five (5) schools were reported damaged in Davao del Sur, General Santos City, and South Cotabato.

Landslides were also reported in three (3) municipalities in South Cotabato.

Following the magnitude 7.8 earthquake in Sarangani, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. ordered the suspension of classes at all levels across affected areas in Mindanao until further notice.

STATE OF CALAMITY:

  • The City of General Santos has declared a state of calamity.

As of the latest PHIVOLCS report released today, a total of 1,055 aftershocks have been recorded following the magnitude 7.8 earthquake in Sarangani. Of these, 301 aftershocks were plotted/located, while 21 were felt by residents in affected areas. The recorded aftershocks ranged from magnitude 1.3 to 6.7.

title: IDN: Drought - 06-2026 - Anticipatory Action: Severe Drought Risk due to El Niño and Positive IOD - Indonesia 2026 (2026-06-09)
content:
Risk Analysis

Indonesia is forecasted to experience prolonged dry conditions during the 2026 dry season due to the combined influence of El Niño conditions and a positive Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD). According to BMKG, the dry season is expected to begin earlier than normal in many regions, with 57.2% of seasonal zones (ZOM) predicted to experience a longer dry season and 64.5% of Indonesia forecasted to receive below-normal rainfall accumulation during the June–September period. The provinces considered most at risk include Central Java, East Java, DI Yogyakarta, West Nusa Tenggara (NTB), East Nusa Tenggara (NTT), West Java, Banten, South Sulawesi, Lampung, Bali, and parts of Kalimantan and Sulawesi. Forecasts indicate a high probability of very low rainfall (<50 mm/month) across these regions between June and October 2026, increasing the likelihood of water shortages, crop failure, reduced agricultural productivity, public health concerns, and increased risk of forest and land fires. Historical operational data from PMI’s drought response in 2023 showed significant humanitarian impacts, including prolonged clean water distribution operations across 131 districts/cities in 21 provinces with more than 93 million litres of water distributed. Provinces such as Central Java, East Java, NTB, and DI Yogyakarta recorded the highest operational demand, indicating high exposure and recurring vulnerability to drought conditions. The projected impacts for 2026 include: o Reduced access to safe water for domestic use and sanitation; o Increased reliance on water trucking and emergency water supply systems; o Livelihood disruption, particularly among rain-fed farming communities; o Increased heat-related illnesses and water-borne disease risks due to limited clean water access; o Potential worsening of forest and land fire risks in parts of Kalimantan and Sulawesi; o Increased economic pressure on vulnerable households due to rising water and food costs. The most vulnerable groups include low-income households, rural farming communities, women-headed households, children, older persons, persons with disabilities, and communities living in drought-prone and water-scarce areas. Coastal communities in some areas may also experience saline water intrusion as river discharge decreases during prolonged dry periods.

Request For Assistance

Government Requests International Assistance: No

NS Requests International Assistance: No

Information Bulletin Published

No

Actions taken by National Society

Summary

Early Actions Taken by National Society (PMI) A. Early Action Phase • Assessment & Planning: o Conducting Enhanced Vulnerability and Capacity Assessment (EVCA) to develop the Emergency Plan of Action (EPOA) for Early Action and Response. o Sectoral focus: WASH, Livelihoods, Health, Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR), and Multi-Purpose Cash Grants (MPCG). • Pre-positioning of Water Tanker Fleets: Deploying clean water tankers to strategic locations. • Logistics Pre-positioning in PMI Warehouses: o Water storage tanks (Tandon), pipes, and jerrycans. o Health kits: Face masks and Abate (larvicide). o Rainwater harvesting equipment (communal systems for NTT province). o Plumbing supplies: Gutters, L-bow pipes, water taps, and filters. • Smoke-Free House Support (Safe Houses): Preparedness for West and Central Kalimantan (subject to justification), including: o Beds, Air Purifiers, Oxygen cylinders, AC units, and Generator sets (Genset). • Hygiene Promotion & Education: o Clean and Healthy Living Behavior (PHBS) campaigns. o Water conservation awareness. o Education on heatstroke and heat-exhaustion prevention. • Community-Based Surveillance (CBS): Monitoring health risks at the village level. • Infrastructure Preparation: o Emergency piping and rainwater harvesting systems. o Deep well/borewell construction (subject to technical justification). o Cleaning and rehabilitation of communal rainwater harvesting tanks (PAH) and village retention basins (embung). • Capacity Building: Training for volunteers and staff in WASH and hygiene promotion. • Cross-Cutting Interventions: o Cash and Voucher Assistance (CVA) preparation. o Community Engagement and Accountability (CEA). o Protection, Gender, and Inclusion (PGI) & Safeguarding. • National Society Development (NSD): Personnel costs (salaries/insurance), operational costs, PMER (Planning, Monitoring, Evaluation, and Reporting), Overhead (OHC), PPE, and visibility. • Post-Distribution Monitoring (PDM): Establishing frameworks for sectoral monitoring. B. Emergency Response Phase • Water Supply: Large-scale clean water distribution (water trucking). • Health Services: o Operation of Smoke-Free Houses (Safe Houses) in West and Central Kalimantan. o Mobile health services and continued Community-Based Surveillance (CBS). • Multi-Purpose Cash Grants (MPCG): Prioritized for livelihood protection (mitigation for crop failure/agricultural loss) and household water purchasing. • Community Engagement: Strengthening CEA and PGI protocols during response. • Support Services: NSD (operational support, insurance, lessons learned workshops), and sectoral Post-Distribution Monitoring (PDM). C. Recovery Phase • Sustainable WASH: o Establishment and empowerment of Community WASH Committees. o Maintenance and protection of natural water springs. • Livelihood Recovery: Providing vocational training for farmers for the upcoming planting season. • Institutional Strengthening: Continued National Society Development (NSD). • DRR & Resilience: Strengthening the Sibat (Community-based disaster volunteers) network and local Disaster Risk Reduction initiatives.

Actions taken by Federation

General

Monitor Situation

Summary: IFRC CCD is monitoring and coordinating closely with PMI NHQ for further update from the field and for further support if required

Actions taken by others

1. Early Warning & Monitoring (BMKG): BMKG (Meteorological, Climatological, and Geophysical Agency) is providing regular seasonal updates and climate outlooks. They are monitoring the El Niño and Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) indicators to provide localized forecasts for regional governments. 2. Coordination & Emergency Status (BNPB/BPBD): The National Disaster Management Authority (BNPB) is coordinating with regional agencies (BPBD) to declare "Emergency Alert" (Siaga Darurat) status in provinces like Central Java, East Java, and NTB. This allows for the mobilization of emergency funds and resources. 3. Weather Modification (TMC): BNPB, in collaboration with the National Research and Innovation Agency (BRIN) and the Indonesian Air Force, is preparing Weather Modification Technology (TMC/Cloud Seeding) to trigger rainfall over strategic reservoirs and fire-prone areas in Kalimantan and Sumatra. 4. Water Infrastructure Management (Ministry of Public Works/PUPR): The Ministry of Public Works and Housing is monitoring water levels in major dams and reservoirs. They are prioritizing water allocation for domestic consumption over irrigation and mobilizing mobile water treatment units to critical areas. 5. Agricultural Support (Ministry of Agriculture): The government is distributing water pumps to farming communities and promoting the use of drought-resistant seed varieties. They are also activating crop insurance schemes (AUTP) to compensate farmers facing harvest failures. 6. Forest Fire Prevention (KLHK): The Ministry of Environment and Forestry has activated forest fire task forces (Manggala Agni) to monitor hotspots and conduct land wetting in peatland areas to prevent fires during the prolonged dry season.
